claim: Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer in men worldwide.
source: Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in men worldwide (Torre et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Torre et al., 2015

claim: Prostate cancer is the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in men worldwide.
source: Prostate cancer is the second most common cancer and the fifth leading cause of cancer-related death in men worldwide (Torre et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Torre et al., 2015

claim: Deregulated androgen receptor (AR) signaling is a major driver of prostate cancer.
source: Deregulated androgen receptor (AR) signaling is a major driver of prostate cancer (Taylor et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taylor et al., 2010

claim: Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is used to treat locally advanced and metastatic prostate cancer.
source: Consequently, androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is used to treat locally advanced and metastatic prostate cancer, achieving remission in most patients.
evidence: Based on established clinical practice and knowledge

claim: ADT achieves remission in most prostate cancer patients.
source: Consequently, androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) is used to treat locally advanced and metastatic prostate cancer, achieving remission in most patients.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge

claim: Prostate cancer inevitably progresses to a castration-resistant state despite castrate-levels of androgens in the serum.
source: However, despite castrate-levels of androgens in the serum, the disease inevitably progresses to a castration-resistant state (Perlmutter and Lepor, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perlmutter and Lepor, 2007

claim: AR signaling remains a pivotal driver in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC).
source: AR signaling remains a pivotal driver in castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), which is illustrated by the efficacy of AR-directed drugs such as abiraterone and enzalutamide.
evidence: Supported by inference from the efficacy of AR-directed drugs

claim: Patients develop resistance to AR-directed drugs and invariably succumb to the disease.
source: Unfortunately, patients develop resistance to these drugs and invariably succumb to the disease (Clegg et al., 2012; Beer et al., 2014; Chi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clegg et al., 2012; Beer et al., 2014; Chi et al., 2019

claim: Mutations in AR are a proposed resistance mechanism to AR inhibitors.
source: Several resistance mechanisms to AR inhibitors have been proposed, including mutations in AR (Korpal et al., 2013; Joseph et al., 2013; Prekovic et al., 2016; Prekovic et al., 2018) and expression of splice variants (Li et al., 2013; Antonarakis et al., 2014; Culig, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Korpal et al., 2013; Joseph et al., 2013; Prekovic et al., 2016; Prekovic et al., 2018

claim: Expression of AR splice variants is a proposed resistance mechanism to AR inhibitors.
source: Several resistance mechanisms to AR inhibitors have been proposed, including mutations in AR (Korpal et al., 2013; Joseph et al., 2013; Prekovic et al., 2016; Prekovic et al., 2018) and expression of splice variants (Li et al., 2013; Antonarakis et al., 2014; Culig, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2013; Antonarakis et al., 2014; Culig, 2017

claim: The F877L missense mutation in AR confers resistance to enzalutamide and apalutamide.
source: For example, the F877L missense mutation in AR was shown to confer resistance to enzalutamide and apalutamide (Korpal et al., 2013; Joseph et al., 2013; Balbas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Korpal et al., 2013; Joseph et al., 2013; Balbas et al., 2013

claim: Upregulation of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) is associated with clinical resistance to enzalutamide.
source: Upregulation of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR, gene symbol NR3C1) was shown to be associated with clinical resistance to enzalutamide (Arora et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arora et al., 2013

claim: AR and GR have overlapping cistromes and transcriptomes in the LREX model.
source: Using the preclinical model LREX (LNCaP/AR Resistant to Enzalutamide Xenograft derived), it was shown that AR and GR have overlapping cistromes and transcriptomes, allowing GR to drive enzalutamide-resistant growth by regulating expression of a subset of AR target genes. (Arora et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arora et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2017

claim: GR drives enzalutamide-resistant growth by regulating expression of a subset of AR target genes.
source: Using the preclinical model LREX (LNCaP/AR Resistant to Enzalutamide Xenograft derived), it was shown that AR and GR have overlapping cistromes and transcriptomes, allowing GR to drive enzalutamide-resistant growth by regulating expression of a subset of AR target genes. (Arora et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arora et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2017

claim: Significant overlap exists between AR and GR cistromes and transcription programs in prostate cancer cells.
source: Significant overlap between AR and GR cistromes and transcription programs in prostate cancer cells was also described by others (Sahu et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sahu et al., 2013

claim: GR upregulation occurs through abrogation of the repressive function of AR and EZH2-mediated methylation of the GR enhancer.
source: GR upregulation was found to occur through abrogation of the repressive function of AR and EZH2-mediated methylation of the GR enhancer (Shah et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shah et al., 2017

claim: A genome-scale approach aimed at identifying novel regulators of AR inhibitor sensitivity has not been reported.
source: However, to the best of our knowledge, a genome-scale approach aimed at identifying novel regulators of AR inhibitor sensitivity has hitherto not been reported.
evidence: Based on authors' knowledge of the literature

claim: Loss-of-function genetic screens facilitate the unbiased identification of genes that have a central role in biological processes.
source: Loss-of-function genetic screens facilitate the unbiased identification of genes that have a central role in biological processes in various genetic and pharmacological backgrounds.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about genetic screening methods

claim: Large-scale gene perturbation experiments are a powerful tool to identify novel drug targets and biomarkers of drug response.
source: Consequently, large-scale gene perturbation experiments are a powerful tool to identify novel drug targets and biomarkers of drug response (Mullenders and Bernards, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mullenders and Bernards, 2009

claim: A genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen identified TLE3 as a modulator of AR inhibitor sensitivity.
source: Through a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen we identified transducin-like enhancer of split 3 (TLE3) as a modulator of AR inhibitor sensitivity that, upon loss, confers resistance to enzalutamide in prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen described in the manuscript

claim: TLE3 loss confers resistance to enzalutamide in prostate cancer cells.
source: Through a genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen we identified transducin-like enhancer of split 3 (TLE3) as a modulator of AR inhibitor sensitivity that, upon loss, confers resistance to enzalutamide in prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from the genome-wide CRISPR-Cas9 screen and validation experiments

claim: The TLE protein family of transcriptional co-repressors is well-conserved and expressed in the nucleus of metazoans.
source: The well-conserved TLE protein family of transcriptional co-repressors is expressed in the nucleus of metazoans and regulate various biological processes including development, cell metabolism, growth and differentiation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about TLE proteins

claim: TLE protein family members regulate various biological processes including development, cell metabolism, growth and differentiation.
source: The well-conserved TLE protein family of transcriptional co-repressors is expressed in the nucleus of metazoans and regulate various biological processes including development, cell metabolism, growth and differentiation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about TLE proteins

claim: TLE protein family members maintain a silenced chromatin structure at the chromatin.
source: At the chromatin, TLE protein family members maintain a silenced chromatin structure (Agarwal et al., 2015; Chen and Courey, 2000; Cinnamon and Paroush, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Agarwal et al., 2015; Chen and Courey, 2000; Cinnamon and Paroush, 2008

claim: TLE3 is deregulated in hormone-driven breast cancer.
source: TLE3 is deregulated in various cancers including hormone-driven breast cancer (Jangal et al., 2014), colorectal cancer (Yang et al., 2016) and prostate cancer (Nakaya et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jangal et al., 2014

claim: TLE3 is deregulated in colorectal cancer.
source: TLE3 is deregulated in various cancers including hormone-driven breast cancer (Jangal et al., 2014), colorectal cancer (Yang et al., 2016) and prostate cancer (Nakaya et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2016

claim: TLE3 is deregulated in prostate cancer.
source: TLE3 is deregulated in various cancers including hormone-driven breast cancer (Jangal et al., 2014), colorectal cancer (Yang et al., 2016) and prostate cancer (Nakaya et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakaya et al., 2007

claim: LNCaP is an androgen-dependent prostate cancer cell line.
source: The androgen-dependent prostate cancer cell line LNCaP is sensitive to AR inhibitors such as apalutamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and enzalutamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), making it a model system well-suited for the unbiased discovery of novel regulators of AR inhibitor sensitivity in prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about LNCaP cells

claim: LNCaP cells are sensitive to apalutamide.
source: The androgen-dependent prostate cancer cell line LNCaP is sensitive to AR inhibitors such as apalutamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and enzalutamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), making it a model system well-suited for the unbiased discovery of novel regulators of AR inhibitor sensitivity in prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: LNCaP cells are sensitive to enzalutamide.
source: The androgen-dependent prostate cancer cell line LNCaP is sensitive to AR inhibitors such as apalutamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and enzalutamide (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), making it a model system well-suited for the unbiased discovery of novel regulators of AR inhibitor sensitivity in prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: LNCaP cells were infected with a lentiviral pool containing the genome-wide scale CRISPR Knock-Out (GeCKO) half-library A targeting 19052 genes with 3 gRNAs per gene.
source: LNCaP cells were infected with a lentiviral pool containing the genome-wide scale CRISPR Knock-Out (GeCKO) half-library A (Sanjana et al., 2014), targeting 19052 genes with 3 gRNAs per gene.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used in the study

claim: Infected LNCaP cells were cultured in the presence of vehicle or 2 μM apalutamide for 6 weeks to allow selection of resistant cells.
source: Infected cells were cultured in the presence of vehicle or 2 μM of the AR inhibitor apalutamide for 6 weeks to allow selection of resistant cells.
evidence: Describes the experimental method used in the study

claim: DESeq2 analysis identified TLE3 as the top hit with all three gRNAs enriched in cells treated with apalutamide compared to untreated cells.
source: DESeq2 (Love et al., 2014) analysis (Figure 1—source data 2) and MAGeCK (Li et al., 2014) analysis (Figure 1—source data 3) both identified TLE3 as the top hit with all three gRNAs enriched in cells treated with apalutamide compared to untreated cells (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data analyzed using DESeq2 and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: MAGeCK analysis identified TLE3 as the top hit with all three gRNAs enriched in cells treated with apalutamide compared to untreated cells.
source: DESeq2 (Love et al., 2014) analysis (Figure 1—source data 2) and MAGeCK (Li et al., 2014) analysis (Figure 1—source data 3) both identified TLE3 as the top hit with all three gRNAs enriched in cells treated with apalutamide compared to untreated cells (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data analyzed using MAGeCK and shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C

claim: Abrogation of TLE3 expression using independent single guide RNAs (sgRNAs) conferred resistance to enzalutamide in LNCaP cells.
source: Abrogation of TLE3 expression using independent single guide RNAs (sgRNAs), as well as short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting TLE3, conferred resistance to both enzalutamide and apalutamide in LNCaP cells in long-term growth assays (14 days) with drug concentrations up to 8 μM (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E

claim: Abrogation of TLE3 expression using short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) conferred resistance to enzalutamide in LNCaP cells.
source: Abrogation of TLE3 expression using independent single guide RNAs (sgRNAs), as well as short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting TLE3, conferred resistance to both enzalutamide and apalutamide in LNCaP cells in long-term growth assays (14 days) with drug concentrations up to 8 μM (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E

claim: Abrogation of TLE3 expression using sgRNAs conferred resistance to apalutamide in LNCaP cells.
source: Abrogation of TLE3 expression using independent single guide RNAs (sgRNAs), as well as short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting TLE3, conferred resistance to both enzalutamide and apalutamide in LNCaP cells in long-term growth assays (14 days) with drug concentrations up to 8 μM (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E

claim: Abrogation of TLE3 expression using shRNAs conferred resistance to apalutamide in LNCaP cells.
source: Abrogation of TLE3 expression using independent single guide RNAs (sgRNAs), as well as short hairpin RNAs (shRNAs) targeting TLE3, conferred resistance to both enzalutamide and apalutamide in LNCaP cells in long-term growth assays (14 days) with drug concentrations up to 8 μM (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and E

claim: Enzalutamide is the current standard used in the clinic for the treatment of castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC).
source: Because enzalutamide is the current standard used in the clinic for the treatment of castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC), we used this drug for subsequent experiments.
evidence: Based on established clinical knowledge

claim: TLE3 loss did not confer drug resistance in CWR-R1 and LAPC4 prostate cancer cell lines.
source: As TLE3 loss did not confer drug resistance in these two cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H), we conclude a context-dependency of this mode of resistance that is not commonly observed in all model systems.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H

claim: TLE3-mediated resistance to AR inhibitors is context-dependent and not commonly observed in all model systems.
source: As TLE3 loss did not confer drug resistance in these two cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F–H), we conclude a context-dependency of this mode of resistance that is not commonly observed in all model systems.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing TLE3 loss does not confer resistance in all cell lines tested

claim: TLE3 is a negative regulator of the Wnt pathway.
source: TLE3 is known to be a negative regulator of the Wnt pathway.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about TLE3 function

claim: Analysis of active ß-catenin levels in TLE3KO cells treated with vehicle or enzalutamide revealed no changes compared to control cells.
source: Analysis of active ß-catenin levels and expression of the bona fide Wnt target gene AXIN2 in TLE3KO cells treated with vehicle or enzalutamide revealed no changes compared to control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating Wnt signaling is not altered in this context.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Expression of AXIN2 in TLE3KO cells treated with vehicle or enzalutamide revealed no changes compared to control cells.
source: Analysis of active ß-catenin levels and expression of the bona fide Wnt target gene AXIN2 in TLE3KO cells treated with vehicle or enzalutamide revealed no changes compared to control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating Wnt signaling is not altered in this context.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Wnt signaling is not altered in TLE3KO cells in the context of enzalutamide treatment.
source: Analysis of active ß-catenin levels and expression of the bona fide Wnt target gene AXIN2 in TLE3KO cells treated with vehicle or enzalutamide revealed no changes compared to control cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), indicating Wnt signaling is not altered in this context.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing no changes in ß-catenin and AXIN2

claim: AR is the top transcription factor associated with genes differentially expressed in control cells versus TLE3KO cells in vehicle condition.
source: Enrichment analysis revealed AR as the top transcription factor associated with genes differentially expressed in control cells versus TLE3KO cells in vehicle condition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: AR is the top transcription factor associated with genes differentially expressed in control cells versus TLE3KO cells cultured in the presence of enzalutamide.
source: Genes differentially expressed in control cells versus TLE3KO cells, cultured in the presence of enzalutamide, also shared AR as the top regulator (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Loss of TLE3 rescued expression of androgen-responsive genes in cells exposed to enzalutamide.
source: We validated expression for several of these genes both in the absence and presence of enzalutamide and found that loss of TLE3 rescued expression of these genes in cells exposed to enzalutamide (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental validation data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Overall AR signaling was maintained in the presence of enzalutamide in TLE3KO cells but not in control cells.
source: Overall, AR signaling was maintained in the presence of enzalutamide in TLE3KO cells but not in control cells, implying a rescue of AR signaling despite enzalutamide treatment (Figure 2D and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 2D and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: TLE3KO cells show a rescue of AR signaling despite enzalutamide treatment.
source: Overall, AR signaling was maintained in the presence of enzalutamide in TLE3KO cells but not in control cells, implying a rescue of AR signaling despite enzalutamide treatment (Figure 2D and E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Inferred from GSEA data showing maintained AR signaling in TLE3KO cells treated with enzalutamide

claim: TLE3 expression is induced by enzalutamide in wild-type LNCaP cells.
source: Indeed, western blot analysis showed that in wild-type (WT) cells, the expression of TLE3 is induced by enzalutamide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: Stimulation with the synthetic androgen R1881 led to a decrease in TLE3 protein levels in LNCaP cells.
source: Conversely, stimulation with the synthetic androgen R1881 led to a decrease in TLE3 protein levels (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F

claim: Both TLE3 and AR bind at enhancer sites of the TLE3 gene.
source: Analysis of publicly available ChIP-seq data (Stelloo et al., 2018) revealed binding of both TLE3 and AR at enhancer sites of the TLE3 gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) suggesting that these transcription factors regulate TLE3 expression, indicating a feedback loop controlling TLE3 transcription.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data from Stelloo et al., 2018 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1H

claim: TLE3 and AR regulate TLE3 expression, indicating a feedback loop controlling TLE3 transcription.
source: Analysis of publicly available ChIP-seq data (Stelloo et al., 2018) revealed binding of both TLE3 and AR at enhancer sites of the TLE3 gene (Figure 2—figure supplement 1H) suggesting that these transcription factors regulate TLE3 expression, indicating a feedback loop controlling TLE3 transcription.
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-seq data showing TLE3 and AR binding at TLE3 gene enhancers

claim: TLE3 mRNA levels are downregulated over time in LNCaP cells treated with R1881.
source: This is supported by analysis of publicly available RNA-seq data (Massie et al., 2011 ) showing that TLE3 mRNA levels are downregulated over time in LNCaP cells that are treated with R1881 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data from Massie et al., 2011 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1I

claim: TLE3 loss does not affect AR gene expression in LNCaP cells.
source: Finally, we also investigated the effect of TLE3 loss on AR gene expression using qPCR and found no differential expression for AR mRNA between control and TLE3KO cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1J

claim: TLE3 binds together with FOXA1 at androgen response elements (AREs).
source: Recently, protein interactome profiling of AR revealed that TLE3 binds together with FOXA1 at androgen response elements (AREs) (Stelloo et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stelloo et al., 2018

claim: Genes showing the strongest log2 fold-change expression in TLE3KO compared to control cells were bound by TLE3.
source: Genes showing the strongest log2 fold-change expression in TLE3KO compared to control cells were indeed bound by TLE3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Co-binding of TLE3 and AR was enriched at loci of differentially expressed genes when compared to a random geneset.
source: We found that co-binding of TLE3 and AR was enriched at loci of the differentially expressed geneset when compared to a random geneset (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq peak enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: Significantly enriched sequence motifs at TLE3 binding sites of differentially expressed genes included members of the forkhead box transcription factor family (including FOXA1), AR, HOXB13 and the glucocorticoid receptor (GR).
source: Furthermore, significantly enriched sequence motifs at TLE3 binding sites of differentially expressed genes included members of the forkhead box transcription factor family (including FOXA1), AR, HOXB13 and the glucocorticoid receptor (GR) (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis data in Supplementary file 1

claim: Loss of TLE3 alters expression of androgen-responsive genes towards an active-AR-like profile in spite of anti-hormonal treatment.
source: Since TLE3 acts as a repressor, the chromatin binding profiles for TLE3, FOXA1 and AR substantiate the expression data indicating that loss of TLE3 alters expression of androgen-responsive genes towards an active-AR-like profile in spite of anti-hormonal treatment, thereby allowing continued growth when these cells are exposed to enzalutamide.
evidence: Inferred from chromatin binding profiles and expression data

claim: Loss of TLE3 allows continued growth of cells exposed to enzalutamide.
source: Since TLE3 acts as a repressor, the chromatin binding profiles for TLE3, FOXA1 and AR substantiate the expression data indicating that loss of TLE3 alters expression of androgen-responsive genes towards an active-AR-like profile in spite of anti-hormonal treatment, thereby allowing continued growth when these cells are exposed to enzalutamide.
evidence: Inferred from chromatin binding profiles, expression data, and proliferation assays

claim: GR was one of the most upregulated genes upon enzalutamide treatment in a TLE3-loss background.
source: Gene expression analysis revealed that GR was one of the most upregulated genes upon enzalutamide treatment in a TLE3-loss background (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 2B and C

claim: Western blot analysis confirmed GR upregulation on protein level in TLE3KO cells treated with enzalutamide.
source: Western blot analysis for GR confirmed this upregulation on protein level (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A

claim: TLE3 and AR bind at the GR enhancer.
source: The binding of TLE3 and AR at the GR enhancer provides further evidence that both proteins play a role in the transcriptional repression of GR (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B

claim: TLE3 and AR play a role in the transcriptional repression of GR.
source: The binding of TLE3 and AR at the GR enhancer provides further evidence that both proteins play a role in the transcriptional repression of GR (Figure 4B).
evidence: Inferred from ChIP-seq data showing TLE3 and AR binding at GR enhancer

claim: TLE3 and AR binding at the GR locus occurs at the same regulatory element described previously to be relevant in the regulation of GR in prostate cancer progression.
source: Moreover, TLE3 and AR binding at this region occurs at the same regulatory element described previously to be relevant in the regulation of GR in prostate cancer progression (Shah et al., 2017) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and citation to Shah et al., 2017

claim: The core GR and AR consensus sequences are highly similar.
source: The core GR and AR consensus sequences are highly similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and GR sequence motifs were enriched at genes differentially expressed in control versus TLE3KO cells cultured with enzalutamide (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: GR sequence motifs were enriched at genes differentially expressed in control versus TLE3KO cells cultured with enzalutamide.
source: The core GR and AR consensus sequences are highly similar (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), and GR sequence motifs were enriched at genes differentially expressed in control versus TLE3KO cells cultured with enzalutamide (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis data in Supplementary file 1

claim: Inhibition of GR using shRNAs in TLE3KO cells resensitized TLE3KO cells to enzalutamide.
source: Inhibition of GR using shRNAs in control and TLE3KO cells resensitized TLE3KO cells to enzalutamide (Figure 4C–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: Inhibition of GR using mifepristone in conjunction with enzalutamide reduced the proliferation of TLE3KO cells when compared to single-drug treatments.
source: Inhibition of GR using the small molecule inhibitor mifepristone in conjunction with enzalutamide, reduced the proliferation of TLE3KO when compared to single-drug treatments (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F

claim: GR binds at chromatin sites proximal to several of the most-differentially expressed genes in control versus TLE3KO cells in the presence of enzalutamide.
source: We next performed ChIP-qPCR to determine GR chromatin binding proximal to several of the most-differentially expressed genes in control versus TLE3KO cells, in the presence of enzalutamide (listed in Figure 2B). This experiment showed binding of GR at these loci only in TLE3KO cells treated with enzalutamide (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4G

claim: Loss of TLE3 resulted in an upregulation of H3K27 acetylation at the GR locus and AR/TLE3 target gene RND3.
source: As TLE3 is known to recruit HDACs (Chen and Courey, 2000; Cinnamon and Paroush, 2008), we also investigated histone acetylation at the GR locus and AR/TLE3 target gene RND3 and found that loss of TLE3 resulted in an upregulation of H3K27 acetylation at these enhancers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D

claim: TLE3 is known to recruit HDACs.
source: As TLE3 is known to recruit HDACs (Chen and Courey, 2000; Cinnamon and Paroush, 2008), we also investigated histone acetylation at the GR locus and AR/TLE3 target gene RND3 and found that loss of TLE3 resulted in an upregulation of H3K27 acetylation at these enhancers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen and Courey, 2000; Cinnamon and Paroush, 2008

claim: Abrogation of the repressive function mediated by both AR and TLE3 at the GR locus allows for increased expression of GR.
source: Thus, abrogation of the repressive function mediated by both AR and TLE3 at the GR locus allows for increased expression of GR which, in turn, is able to confer enzalutamide resistance by substituting for AR in this context.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing TLE3/AR binding at GR locus, GR upregulation upon TLE3 loss, and GR-mediated resistance

claim: GR is able to confer enzalutamide resistance by substituting for AR.
source: Thus, abrogation of the repressive function mediated by both AR and TLE3 at the GR locus allows for increased expression of GR which, in turn, is able to confer enzalutamide resistance by substituting for AR in this context.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing GR upregulation, GR binding at AR target genes, and resensitization upon GR inhibition

claim: Several of the most-differentially expressed genes (RND3, GNAI1, GR, UGT2B17 and PMP22) overlap with GR-regulated genes described in a model for GR-mediated enzalutamide resistance.
source: Interestingly, we found overlap between several of the most-differentially expressed genes listed in Figure 2 (RND3, GNAI1, GR, UGT2B17 and PMP22) and GR-regulated genes described in a model for GR-mediated enzalutamide resistance as reported by others (Arora et al., 2013) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by comparison with data from Arora et al., 2013 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E

claim: AR and GR have overlapping transcriptomes and cistromes in the LNCaP-derived enzalutamide-resistant cell model LREX.
source: These results are further supported by previous findings showing that AR and GR have overlapping transcriptomes and cistromes in the LNCaP-derived enzalutamide-resistant cell model LREX where GR was shown to confer enzalutamide resistance (Arora et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arora et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2017

claim: GR confers enzalutamide resistance in the LREX model.
source: These results are further supported by previous findings showing that AR and GR have overlapping transcriptomes and cistromes in the LNCaP-derived enzalutamide-resistant cell model LREX where GR was shown to confer enzalutamide resistance (Arora et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arora et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2017

claim: Loss of TLE3 in conjunction with AR inhibition results in GR upregulation, leading to enzalutamide-resistance in LNCaP prostate cancer cells.
source: Together, our data shows that loss of TLE3 in conjunction with AR inhibition results in GR upregulation, leading to enzalutamide-resistance in LNCaP prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental data including gene expression, western blot, ChIP, and proliferation assays

claim: TLE3 expression and GR expression are inversely correlated in biopsy samples from prostate cancer patients with early-stage disease.
source: Analysis of two publicly available RNA-seq datasets (TCGA prostate and Abida et al., 2019 ) revealed an inverse correlation between TLE3 expression and GR expression in biopsy samples from prostate cancer patients with early-stage disease (Figure 5A) as well as advanced prostate cancer (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: TLE3 expression and GR expression are inversely correlated in biopsy samples from prostate cancer patients with advanced prostate cancer.
source: Analysis of two publicly available RNA-seq datasets (TCGA prostate and Abida et al., 2019 ) revealed an inverse correlation between TLE3 expression and GR expression in biopsy samples from prostate cancer patients with early-stage disease (Figure 5A) as well as advanced prostate cancer (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: TLE3 expression is a prognostic factor for prostate cancer patients treated with anti-hormonal therapy.
source: Analysis of the TCGA prostate cancer patient dataset filtered for patients who had undergone anti-hormonal therapy revealed a correlation between TLE3 expression and biochemical recurrence (p = 0.033, n = 65) (Figure 5C). These data show that TLE3 expression is a prognostic factor for prostate cancer patients treated with anti-hormonal therapy.
evidence: Supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Low TLE3 expression correlates with biochemical recurrence in prostate cancer patients treated with anti-hormonal therapy.
source: Analysis of the TCGA prostate cancer patient dataset filtered for patients who had undergone anti-hormonal therapy revealed a correlation between TLE3 expression and biochemical recurrence (p = 0.033, n = 65) (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Two CRPC patients with short PSA response to enzalutamide (<6 months) had moderate to high GR expression at baseline with weak or negative staining for TLE3.
source: Two patients had a short PSA response to enzalutamide (<6 months), without radiological response. Tumor tissue of these patients showed moderate to high GR expression at baseline with weak or negative staining for TLE3 (Figure 5D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: For one CRPC patient with short response to enzalutamide, the inverse association between TLE3 and GR became more pronounced upon enzalutamide treatment.
source: Moreover, for one of these patients, the inverse association between TLE3 and GR became more pronounced upon enzalutamide treatment (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D

claim: A CRPC patient with profound response to enzalutamide (PSA response >12 months, radiological response) had weak staining for TLE3 and moderate staining for GR at baseline.
source: The third patient, having a more profound response (PSA response >12 months, radiological response), had weak staining for TLE3 and moderate staining for GR at baseline.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data

claim: In a CRPC patient with profound response to enzalutamide, TLE3 was low and GR expression had increased in post-treatment tissue.
source: In the post-treatment staining, TLE3 was low, whereas GR expression had increased (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D

claim: A CRPC patient with protracted response to enzalutamide (>2 years) showed low expression of both TLE3 and GR in pre- and post-treatment tissue.
source: The fourth patient had a protracted response to enzalutamide (>2 years) and showed low expression of both TLE3 and GR in pre- and post-treatment tissue (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: In a CRPC patient with protracted response to enzalutamide, amplification of AR was observed upon treatment.
source: In this patient, amplification of AR was observed upon treatment, potentially explaining resistance not related to TLE3 expression.
evidence: Supported by clinical observation

claim: TLE3 and GR are inversely correlated in prostate cancer patient samples.
source: Combined, these data show that TLE3 and GR are inversely correlated in prostate cancer patient samples and that low TLE3 and high GR expression were observed in several cases of enzalutamide resistance.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis and immunohistochemistry data from patient samples

claim: Low TLE3 and high GR expression were observed in several cases of enzalutamide resistance.
source: Combined, these data show that TLE3 and GR are inversely correlated in prostate cancer patient samples and that low TLE3 and high GR expression were observed in several cases of enzalutamide resistance.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data from CRPC patient samples

claim: TLE3 co-localizes with FOXA1 and AR at enhancer elements which are selectively activated during prostate tumorigenesis.
source: TLE3 was shown to co-localize with FOXA1 and AR at enhancer elements, which are selectively activated during prostate tumorigenesis (Stelloo et al., 2018), underscoring the importance of these transcription factors in this context.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stelloo et al., 2018

claim: Loss of TLE3 results in an active-AR-like profile despite anti-hormonal treatment.
source: Our gene expression analyses show that loss of TLE3 results in an active-AR-like profile despite anti-hormonal treatment.
evidence: Supported by gene expression and GSEA data presented in the manuscript

claim: TLE3 acts as a co-repressor in breast cancer cells where it co-regulates the expression of a subset of ERα target genes.
source: Similarly, TLE3 was described as a co-repressor in breast cancer cells, where it co-regulates the expression of a subset of ERα target genes (Jangal et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jangal et al., 2014

claim: The binding of TLE3 to the chromatin at ERα target genes was dependent on FOXA1 in breast cancer cells.
source: The same study showed that the binding of TLE3 to the chromatin at ERα target genes was dependent on FOXA1 (Jangal et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jangal et al., 2014

claim: Pathway reactivation or feedback activation of parallel signaling pathways are commonly described mechanisms found in drug-resistant tumors treated with targeted therapy.
source: Pathway reactivation or feedback activation of parallel signaling pathways are commonly described mechanisms found in drug-resistant tumors treated with targeted therapy (Prahallad et al., 2012; Pawar et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Prahallad et al., 2012; Pawar et al., 2018

claim: GR upregulation in the LREX model was not immediate in response to enzalutamide but required treatment with the drug for an extended amount of time for adaptation in vitro.
source: In this study, the GR upregulation observed in the preclinical LREX model was not immediate in response to enzalutamide but required treatment with the drug for an extended amount of time for adaptation in vitro (Arora et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arora et al., 2013

claim: The extended period of time needed for GR upregulation in the LREX model could suggest an acquired loss of TLE3 expression over time.
source: This extended period of time needed for adaptation could suggest an acquired loss of TLE3 expression over time, resulting in deregulated GR expression.
evidence: Speculative inference based on the authors' findings and previous literature

claim: Loss of the repressive signals of both AR binding and EZH2-mediated methylation of a tissue-specific enhancer at the GR locus lead to upregulation of GR and drug resistance in prostate cancer cells.
source: The work of Shah et al. (2017) showed that loss of the repressive signals of both AR binding and EZH2-mediated methylation of a tissue-specific enhancer at the GR locus lead to upregulation of GR and drug resistance in prostate cancer cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to Shah et al., 2017

claim: TLE3 is able to bind the same GR enhancer as AR and EZH2.
source: TLE3 is a known transcriptional repressor and is able to bind the same GR enhancer (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: TLE3 loss, in conjunction with AR inhibition, leads to GR upregulation.
source: Our finding that TLE3 loss, in conjunction with AR inhibition, leads to GR upregulation provides deeper insight into the epigenetic regulation of the GR locus in prostate cancer cells and supports the previously undescribed role of TLE3 in conferring enzalutamide sensitivity via GR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data including gene expression, western blot, and ChIP analyses

claim: TLE3 has a previously undescribed role in conferring enzalutamide sensitivity via GR.
source: Our finding that TLE3 loss, in conjunction with AR inhibition, leads to GR upregulation provides deeper insight into the epigenetic regulation of the GR locus in prostate cancer cells and supports the previously undescribed role of TLE3 in conferring enzalutamide sensitivity via GR.
evidence: Based on the novel findings presented in the manuscript

claim: The availability of in vitro prostate cancer models is limited.
source: The availability of in vitro prostate cancer models is limited, and the heterogeneous nature of resistance mechanisms to antihormonal therapies in prostate cancer may explain why TLE3 loss did not confer resistance to enzalutamide in LAPC4 and CWR-R1 cells.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about prostate cancer models

claim: The heterogeneous nature of resistance mechanisms to antihormonal therapies in prostate cancer may explain why TLE3 loss did not confer resistance to enzalutamide in LAPC4 and CWR-R1 cells.
source: The availability of in vitro prostate cancer models is limited, and the heterogeneous nature of resistance mechanisms to antihormonal therapies in prostate cancer may explain why TLE3 loss did not confer resistance to enzalutamide in LAPC4 and CWR-R1 cells.
evidence: Speculative explanation for experimental observations

claim: The clinical implications of TLE3 expression in prostate cancer are yet to be resolved and need to be determined in larger cohorts.
source: Although these observations are in agreement with our hypothesis, the clinical implications of our findings are yet to be resolved and need to be determined in larger cohorts.
evidence: Authors' acknowledgment of study limitations

claim: The findings warrant further investigation into the role of TLE3 and enzalutamide resistance in prostate cancer patients.
source: Thus, our results warrant further investigation into the role of TLE3 and enzalutamide resistance in prostate cancer patients.
evidence: Authors' recommendation based on their findings

claim: Apalutamide is a next-generation AR inhibitor structurally similar to enzalutamide.
source: The screen was performed using apalutamide (SPARTAN Investigators et al., 2018), which is a next-generation AR inhibitor structurally similar to enzalutamide.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about apalutamide and citation to SPARTAN Investigators et al., 2018
